To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the use of trusted hardware primitives such as Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX) can be used to build trusted components of modern application that can provide strong confidentiality guarantees, 2) the trusted hardware primitives are vulnerable to side channel attacks and thus require careful use, and 3) the use of formal verification techniques to certify confidentiality can help reduce the risk of programming errors and side channels leaks in trusted components.

1) the Intel SGX platform is vulnerable to a large number of side channel leaks that are not addressed by current software and hardware defenses, 2) the Sanctum platform provides a more secure execution environment than Intel SGX, but is vulnerable to a few side channel leaks and 3) we can automatically verify confidentiality of enclave programs against a large number of leaks, including those that are not addressed in current software and hardware solutions, thus providing a more comprehensive solution than prior work.

(i) Intel SGX and Sanctum provide strong security guarantees against privileged adversaries, (ii) Intel SGX is a promising platform for building applications that ensure confidentiality in the presence of privileged adversaries, (iii) the formal framework and verification tools developed in this thesis can be used to certify that applications running on Intel SGX do not leak secrets, and (iv) Intel SGX can be used to build applications with provable security guarantees, even in presence of a privileged attacker.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing and evaluating tools for verifying the confidentiality of software running in trusted hardware platforms.
building secure computing systems by combining the best of hardware and software.
the design and implementation of a secure computing platform, and its application to real world systems and applications.

this thesis makes significant contributions to the field of secure computing, including formal threat models, formal models of trusted platforms (such as Intel SGX) and formal semantics for enclave execution.
we present a new approach for developing and certifying confidentiality properties of applications that rely on trusted hardware primitives such as Intel's SGX.
the thesis presents a new approach for building and verifying secure applications using trusted primitives.

we have developed a formal framework for modeling enclave execution and a suite of tools and techniques that can be used to verify confidentiality properties (in particular, lack of explicit leaks and certain side-channel leaks) of programs that use Intel SGX.
this dissertation makes significant contributions to building secure systems using certified software and trusted hardware.

we provide a formal framework and techniques for reasoning about confidentiality properties of enclave applications and we show that the techniques can be used to certify the confidentiality of real world applications.

we are able to certify confidentiality properties in a practical manner.
it is possible to build and verify secure applications that use trusted hardware primitives such as enclaves.
